html:
Live in one country for a while and then move to another, and you notice a lot of interesting things, both from the inside and from the outside. Some of your views get stronger; others no longer hold. Here, based on my own experience and opinions, are a few things about Germany.

The Germans

Germans are definitely a breed apart in Europe. The classic stereotype: anywhere outside Germany, if you do something in a rigid, by-the-book way, someone will say, “You are so German!” Inflexible, meticulous, sometimes to a fault: that’s the first impression Europe, and the world, has of Germany. A few fun stories:

— On a business trip I shared a twin room with a German colleague. One night there was a mosquito in the room, and I got up to swat it. He woke up, saw what I was doing, reached into his suitcase and pulled out a bag: mosquito repellent spray, a lotion to put on your skin, and a cream for after you’ve been bitten. The full kit. I was stunned. He calmly said, “I’m German,” turned over and went back to sleep, the unsung hero. And that’s before I mention that he brought five shirts to the conference. Let’s just say it was his first international conference and he didn’t know any better…

— At the institute’s farewell party for a colleague, everyone was having a blast on the lawn outside the building, with music blaring from big speakers, going wild half the night; some colleagues, men and women, were even dancing up close. Around midnight, when things were winding down, someone said, “Let’s start cleaning up!” Every smile vanished, everyone turned back into their daytime selves, and they set about clearing up the mess. Another foreign colleague and I wondered whether they’d only been pretending to be drunk. Before and after a drink, at work and after hours, they’re like different people, a bit like the Japanese. Though the Japanese go even further: after work, at karaoke, they’re wild before they’ve even started drinking.

— Sie sind in Deutschland! Sie müssen Deutsch lernen! (You’re in Germany! You must learn German!) There are far too many examples of this one, so I’ll leave it there.

— At an intersection in the middle of the night, not a car in sight, the pedestrian light is red, and everyone waits. That would never happen in the Netherlands: people cross on red even in broad daylight. They don’t give a shit.

— Political correctness. The Führer and the Nazis almost never come up. Once a secretary mentioned them by accident and said “Entschuldigung” (sorry) to thin air. Another time, a German colleague said to a Jewish colleague, “You went home pretty late last night. The light in your office was on the whole time.” The Jewish colleague replied, “Yeah, Arbeit macht frei” (“work sets you free,” the slogan over the gate at Auschwitz). All the Germans fell silent at once, and you could have heard a pin drop. The Jewish colleague was baffled: “It was my ancestors who got hurt!”

— There’s a saying: when a room falls silent, an angel is passing through. The skies over Germany are full of angels. Germans aren’t the least bit afraid of the awkwardness of sitting at a table without talking. Two electricians at our institute shared an office and went up to the kitchen upstairs for coffee at ten o’clock sharp every day. Face to face, they mostly said nothing, unless another colleague came in. Wouldn’t it be better to drink their coffee in the office, where at least having some work in hand would spare them the awkwardness… Oh, right, they’re not afraid of that.

— They love making plans, and sometimes spend longer planning than doing. You can rarely get them to do anything at short notice; everything has to go through the calendar, though the Dutch are just the same. After living in Germany for a long time, I’ve come to think it’s rather a good thing, and I now hate last-minute plans and changes too.

I’ll add more fun stories as I think of them. I think Germans today, taken as a whole, are a contradictory, conflicted lot. Historically there was no such thing as a unified Germany until Bismarck came along. You know what happened next: an economic boom, a world power, the Führer’s rise, a period of glory. Just as national self-confidence peaked, World War II ended. The political winds turned sharply, the Nazis fell from their pedestal, and everyone was taught to be ashamed of that history. So the postwar generation was a generation of shame, feeling they had to answer for the sins of the one before. The slump didn’t last long. The German economy took off again, and a generation or two later the shame is still there but fading, while the self-confidence of citizens of a powerful nation has grown back. So guilt over history, the strong self-confidence that comes with economic power, and strict, finely detailed rules: this subtly conflicting mix is what makes most Germans present themselves to the world the distinctive way they do today. I once talked about Germans with an Italian who grew up in Germany. He said Germans all have a touch of perfectionism: if their English isn’t great, for example, they’d rather not speak it at all than risk their image. I think he has a point. I’m curious how others who have lived in Germany see Germans; feel free to join the discussion.

The German language

All those consonants make German sound very harsh. Speak just a little loudly, no argument needed, and it already sounds like er ist wieder da (“he’s back,” the title of the satirical novel and film about Hitler returning)… Get a taste from the video below (from 0:16; it’s Trevor Noah, a stand-up comedian I really like). A Dutch colleague used to say: you have to admit it, German is the ugliest-sounding language in the world. His wife is German, by the way. But I have to say, I thought so too, until I heard Dutch.

Watch this video in the original Zhihu answer

00:58 Imitating the Führer’s accent

German grammar is hard, too, as anyone who knows a little about Germany will know.

Germany may be small (by China’s standards; in Europe it’s a big country), but it has lots of dialects. Someone from the west who goes to the Bavarian mountains in the south might not understand a word. Then there’s accented Austrian German, Swiss German, Luxembourgish German and more. An extreme example: a German colleague told me that some poorly educated people in remote areas can’t even keep the dative and accusative apart.

Everyday life

Let’s start with the environment. Germany may be all green hills and clear rivers now, but a few decades ago it suffered from smog too, even worse than China today. A German colleague in his sixties told me that when he was little, his family didn’t dare hang the laundry out in the yard, or it would be covered in soot (he grew up in the Ruhr). It has been cleaned up very well since; the Rhine has gone from an open sewer to what it is today. Many cities have banned diesel cars. One thing I couldn’t get used to was the chewing gum all over the streets. At first I couldn’t believe it was gum. Around bus stops it’s especially horrifying.

German products have been hyped to the skies by Germany’s fans; made in Germany is a guarantee of quality. But a hundred years ago, Made in Germany meant much what Made in China means today: cheap, shoddy goods. The British made the Germans put the label on their products to tell German goods apart from British ones. Seen in that light, I have faith in Chinese products: I believe enough quantity eventually turns into quality. Today Germany’s manufacturing and car industries are insanely strong, unrivaled in Europe. Besides the big carmakers, there are suppliers at every tier, more than you could count. The car industry alone provides countless jobs.

As for getting around, Deutsche Bahn has been mocked to death. Since it stopped being state-owned a dozen or so years ago, it has gone downhill fast. Delays have become routine, which really hurts Germany’s image. This has also given rise to the long-distance bus business. Intercity coaches supposedly weren’t allowed in Germany before, but the railways let everyone down. Now Flixbus dominates, having swallowed up MeinFernbus and Postbus, and prices have multiplied from the ten-odd euros of a few years ago. Everyone knows the Autobahn has no speed limit; from the slow lane you often see cars shoot past like bullets in the far-left lane. On a recent business trip in Germany, a colleague hit 220 km/h, and it felt as though we were about to take off. I can do 160 myself without feeling a thing, because everyone is going fast.

Healthcare: before I moved to the Netherlands, I thought German healthcare was terrible. Looking back, it’s expensive, but it really works. In the Netherlands it’s very hard to get your GP to refer you to a hospital; in Germany, if you ask, your GP generally won’t stand in your way. In the end, Germany is a rich country and doesn’t sweat the cost of treatment, and anyway, it all comes out of your own pocket. For my rant about German doctors, see this answer:

What are the frustrations of living in Germany?

Contracts of every kind. Live in Germany for a few years and you’ll have perfected your signature. A contract easily runs to dozens of pages of densely packed rules and regulations, followed by endless signatures. Hardly anyone has the time to read them, so certain tricks slip past. When a problem comes up, they pull out the contract and point to some corner: “It’s in the contract. If you didn’t read it, whose fault is that?” Canceling a contract is a hassle too, and many contracts renew automatically if you forget to cancel them.

The differences between East and West are still there. The Berlin Wall fell 30 years ago, but West German citizens still pay a monthly tax for the East, even though per capita income in Berlin has overtaken the Ruhr. Naturally, many taxpayers are unhappy about it. In the West you also hear snide remarks about East Germans, like someone saying sarcastically that so-and-so is from the East, no wonder they’re like that. That same secretary at the institute has a cousin from the East who moved to the West after reunification. For a long time afterward, the cousin said, she didn’t know what to do with herself: she was so used to being told what to do that sudden freedom left her lost. I’ve recently been bingeing a German series, Deutschland 83, about an East German spy in West Germany. It’s pretty good.


I’ll add more as I think of it. Here are a few more of my answers about Germany:
